blocks.text: I can compare and group materials according to whether they are in {solid}, {liquid} or {gas} state.
In this lesson you will use properties to sort materials into groups.
Tap each word to see what it means.

items.def: A solid has a fixed shape and volume but some solids can change shape when a force is applied.
A liquid can flow, has a fixed volume and takes the shape of the bottom of its container.
A gas can flow, has no fixed volume and takes the shape of the whole of its container.
To classify is to sort objects into groups.
A Venn diagram is a way of displaying how you group items. It is made up of overlapping circles.

blocks.text: **Matter** is the “stuff” that physical things are made from.
Matter can exist in different states. The common states of matter are solid, liquid and gas.
Materials have different properties when they are in different states of matter. They behave in different ways depending on what state they are in.
Materials in the liquid state can flow, have a fixed volume and take the shape of the bottom of their container.
Even when a liquid changes its shape, it always takes up the same amount of space. Liquids have a {fixed volume}.

blocks.label: Are all liquids drinks?
blocks.text: No. There are lots of types of liquids that are not safe to drink, including hand sanitiser, cleaning products, petrol and diesel.
**Solids** have a fixed shape and volume, but some solids can change shape when a force is applied. They always take up the same amount of space and they do not flow like liquids.

**Gases** are often invisible, but they do have properties. A gas escapes from an unsealed container and has no fixed shape or volume. It spreads out and changes its shape and volume to fill up whatever container it is in.

items.q: A marble and an iron pan are both …
Petrol is a liquid. Which of these is a property of petrol?
options: it can flow and has a fixed volume

items.q: A gas is moved into a bigger container. What does the gas do?
options: It stays in a small lump at the bottom
It stays exactly the same shape
It spreads out to fill the whole container

blocks.text: We can observe the properties of different materials and use them to group, or **classify**, them according to their state.

items: If a material has a fixed shape, it is in the solid state.
If a material flows and takes the shape of the bottom of a container, it is in the liquid state.

blocks.text: Example: shampoo can be poured and takes the shape of the bottom of the bottle, so it must be in the liquid state.
We could use three separate sorting circles: one for the solid state, one for the liquid state and one for the gas state.

blocks.q: Use the properties to classify each one as solid, liquid or gas.

blocks.text: Some objects are made of different materials, so they can have properties of more than one state.
Helium is invisible and it has taken the shape of the whole container, which is the balloon.
A **Venn diagram** can be used to group solids, liquids and gases. It has one circle for each state of matter, and the circles are arranged so that they overlap.
The spaces where the circles overlap are used for objects which have properties of {more than one state}.

items: A wooden ruler is in the solid state because it has a fixed shape and volume, so it goes in the solid circle.
A helium balloon goes where the solid and gas circles overlap.
A glass of apple juice goes where the solid and liquid circles overlap.

blocks.label: What is the overlap of the liquid and gas circles for?
blocks.text: It is for objects which have some properties of the gas state and some of the liquid state.

blocks.q: Match each item to its place in the Venn diagram.

pairs.b: where the solid and gas circles overlap
where the solid and liquid circles overlap

blocks.text: Some materials, like sand, are difficult to classify because they appear to have properties of both solids and liquids.
Andeep says: sand flows when I pour it into my bucket, then it fills the shape of the bottom of the bucket, so I will classify sand as a liquid. Do you agree?

blocks.label: Tap to find out
blocks.text: Andeep is incorrect. Each individual part of sand is a tiny grain in the solid state. If you separate out one grain of sand, it has a fixed volume and shape, unless a force changes it.

blocks.label: So why can we pour sand?
blocks.text: When there are lots of solid grains together, they can slide over each other and move like a flowing liquid. If there are enough tiny parts of solid, they take the shape of the bottom of the container, even though they are in the solid state.

blocks.label: How is pouring sand different from pouring a liquid?
blocks.text: When a liquid is poured into a container, it spreads out to fill it to the corners, even if there is only a small volume. When a solid like sand is poured into a container, it often forms a pile, rather than spreading to the corners.

slides.title: Other solids that can be poured

blocks.text: Sugar, salt and rice also appear to have some properties of a liquid, because they fill the bottom of a container and can be poured.
Solids which are made up of many small grains can be poured or take the shape of the bottom of their container.

items.q: One single grain of sand is in which state?
Which of these is a solid that can be poured because it is made of many small grains?

blocks.text: Imagine you classify a digestive biscuit in three different ways.

blocks.label: A whole biscuit
blocks.text: It has the properties of a solid because it did not flow, could be cut or shaped, kept its shape, and always took the same amount of space.

blocks.label: A crushed biscuit
blocks.text: It has some properties of a liquid because the pile of crumbs could be poured between containers. The crumbs spread out in the bottom of the container but formed a pile, like a volcano shape. They did not flow to the edges.

blocks.label: One crumb
blocks.text: It has the properties of a solid because it did not flow, kept its shape, and always took the same amount of space.

items: We can observe and classify materials as being in the solid, liquid or gas state.
Some materials used to make objects can have properties of more than one state.
Some materials are difficult to classify because they appear to have properties of both solids and liquids.
A Venn diagram can be used to group solids, liquids and gases.

flashcards.front: What does it mean to classify?

flashcards.back: A way of displaying how you group items. It is made up of overlapping circles.

flashcards.front: What are the overlapping parts of a Venn diagram of solids, liquids and gases used for?
flashcards.back:
Objects which have properties of more than one state.

Example: a helium balloon (foil is solid, helium is gas).

flashcards.front: How can we tell that shampoo is in the liquid state?
flashcards.back: It can be poured and takes the shape of the bottom of the bottle.
No. Hand sanitiser, cleaning products, petrol and diesel are liquids that are not safe to drink.

flashcards.front: Which material is a football’s outer layer made of, and in which state is it?
flashcards.back: Rubber, in the solid state. It is filled with air, which is in the gas state.

flashcards.front: In which state is the foil of a helium balloon, and in which state is the helium?
flashcards.back: The foil is in the solid state. The helium is in the gas state.

flashcards.front: Why is sand difficult to classify?
flashcards.back: It appears to have properties of both solids and liquids.

flashcards.front: What state is a single grain of sand in?
flashcards.back: The solid state. It has a fixed volume and shape, unless a force changes it.

flashcards.front: Why can sand be poured even though its grains are solid?
flashcards.back: Lots of solid grains together can slide over each other and move like a flowing liquid.

flashcards.front: How is pouring sand different from pouring a liquid?
flashcards.back: A liquid spreads out to fill the container to the corners. Sand often forms a pile.

worksheet.title: Worksheet: Comparing and grouping solids, liquids and gases
worksheet.instructions: Answer each question with a short answer. Use the properties of solids, liquids and gases to classify each material.

questions.prompt: Is a wooden ruler in the solid, liquid or gas state?
questions.explanation: A wooden ruler has a fixed shape and volume, so it is in the solid state.

questions.prompt: Are rain drops in the solid, liquid or gas state?
questions.explanation: Rain drops flow and take the shape of the bottom of a container, so they are liquid.

questions.prompt: Is helium in a balloon in the solid, liquid or gas state?
questions.explanation: Helium is invisible and takes the shape of the whole container, which is the balloon.

questions.prompt: Is a whole digestive biscuit in the solid or the liquid state?
questions.explanation: A whole biscuit does not flow, can be cut or shaped, keeps its shape and always takes the same amount of space.

questions.prompt: Is one single crumb of a crushed biscuit in the solid or the liquid state?
questions.explanation: One crumb does not flow, keeps its shape and always takes the same amount of space.

questions.prompt: What word means ‘to sort objects into groups’?
questions.explanation: To classify is to sort objects into groups.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the type of diagram, made of overlapping circles, that can be used to group solids, liquids and gases?
questions.explanation: A Venn diagram has one circle for each state, and the circles overlap.

questions.prompt: The outer layer of a football is made of rubber. In which state is the rubber?
questions.explanation: The rubber outer layer of a football is in the solid state.

questions.prompt: A football is filled with air. In which state is the air?
questions.explanation: Air is a mixture of gases, so it is in the gas state.

questions.prompt: A Venn diagram for solids, liquids and gases has one circle for each state of matter. How many circles is that?
questions.explanation: There is one circle each for the solid, liquid and gas states.
